lines.text: III
The modern man who no longer builds an altar to the
unknown God has either forgotten God completely and cast
aside the thought of God, or else he has a god who is only
too well known. Just as Paul takes for his starting point the
inscription on the altar, so also he makes use of the philo-
sophical theism entertained in cultured circles, of the outlook
which apprehends God as Him in whom we "live and move
and have our being" and which can proudly affirm: "For
we are indeed His offspring." This was the teaching of the
stoics: the Deity inheres in, flows through, and moulds all
things; it breathes in our breath and courses in our blood.
In this sense the modern man too gladly accepts the state-
ment: "In Him we live and move and have our being." And
this truth moves him like ancient man to devotion and
kindles him to worship the divine energies of the world. The
theme becomes a solemn and soothing musical accompani-
ment to his life, and he does not notice that in this way, by
his very religion, he is resisting God and relegating Him to a
remote distance. For this kind of religion, which proposes to
heap upon man all riches and abundance of life and to set
him in the intricate pattern of a highly organized world, also
wishes to regard the world as a beautiful work of art and
man's veneration for the divine as an integral part of this
living All. In fact it uses man's veneration for the life-forces
which flow through the universe as a means of justifying the
stirrings and strivings of the human will, and it speaks about
the god within man's own breast.
But it does not wish to recognize the true God who con-
fronts man not as a confirmation of his self-centred being
but as a critical force; the living God who stands over against
man and questions him in gift and fate, the Creator-God before
whom man is as nothing, the Judge to whom man is account-
able. God is not the unfateful current of power which streams
through the life of nature, but the Lord of history. He is not
the mysterious power which underlies and encircles all life,
